content: The diagnosis of acute bronchitis is typically based on clinical evaluation, and various clinical definitions have been applied. Currently, there are no clearly effective treatments for the cough associated with acute bronchitis. Beta2-agonists are frequently prescribed, possibly because clinicians suspect that some patients may have reversible airflow obstruction, similar to what is observed in conditions like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which could contribute to their symptoms. The objective of this review was to assess whether beta2-agonists improve symptoms of acute bronchitis in individuals without underlying pulmonary diseases such as asthma, COPD, or pulmonary fibrosis. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and LILACS, covering studies published up to May 2015. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults or children over two years of age with acute bronchitis or acute cough, without known pulmonary disease, who were allocated to receive beta2-agonists versus placebo, no treatment, or alternative treatments. Three review authors independently selected outcomes and extracted data while blinded to the study results. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in each trial. The analysis was stratified by age group, with separate evaluations for children and adults. In children, two trials of moderate quality involving 134 participants without evidence of airflow restriction found no benefits from oral beta2-agonists. In adults, five trials involving 418 participants yielded mixed results. Overall, the summary statistics did not demonstrate significant benefits from either oral (three trials) or inhaled (two trials) beta2-agonists. Specifically, three studies with low-quality evidence showed no significant differences in daily cough scores or in the percentage of adults still coughing after seven days (71% in the control group; risk ratio [RR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63 to 1.18; 220 participants). One trial reported that subgroups with evidence of airflow limitation experienced lower symptom scores when treated with beta2-agonists. Additionally, trials that observed quicker resolution of cough with beta2-agonists tended to include a higher proportion of participants who were wheezing at baseline. However, low-quality evidence also indicated that adults treated with beta2-agonists were more likely to report adverse effects such as tremor, shakiness, or nervousness (RR 7.94, 95% CI 1.17 to 53.94; 211 participants). The number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) was calculated as 2. In conclusion, there is no evidence to support the use of beta2-agonists in children with acute cough who do not exhibit airflow restriction. Similarly, there is little evidence to justify the routine use of beta2-agonists in adults with acute cough. While these agents may provide symptom relief, including cough reduction, in individuals with evidence of airflow restriction, this potential benefit is not strongly supported by the available data. Furthermore, the potential benefits must be carefully weighed against the risk of adverse effects associated with beta2-agonist use.
